name: tabor-cleopatra-staff
title: Cleopatra’s broken staff
description: A provenance file for Nathan Tabor’s account of a broken staff.
sections: The Met catalogs a Roman glass intaglio sometimes identified as Cleopatra VII. It gives a documented comparison object for the period, with the portrait identification treated as tentative.

The British Museum’s bronze coin G.1117 depicts Cleopatra VII. On the reverse, the Greek letter pi marks a denomination of eighty bronze drachmas. The coin provides an example of royal imagery from Cleopatra’s reign.
Was scepters in an Egyptian inlay

The Met dates the glass inlay 10.130.2704 to 100 BCE–100 CE. Its ankh and was scepter imagery provides a comparison for royal and religious symbols around the Ptolemaic–Roman transition. The accession identifies a glass inlay.

The staff’s source, its owner, the account of its breakage, and any fragment inventory remain open. A source with a quoted passage, image caption, or accession number can anchor the first provenance entry.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art object 249300 is a separate Roman glass intaglio, with a tentative identification of Cleopatra VII. It does not identify, authenticate, depict, or establish custody of the broken staff in Nathan Tabor’s account. Do not infer a staff provenance from the portrait comparison.
Identity and chain of custody still unverified

Needed to advance this dossier: a primary source that explicitly identifies the staff; an object or collection accession identifier; an attributed description or image of the alleged break; fragment counts and locations; and dated transfers or inventories. No such evidence is asserted in this record.

Nathan Tabor’s phrase about a broken Cleopatra staff is preserved as his account. The museum citation supports only a separately cataloged comparison object. The staff’s existence, date, ownership and breakage remain unresolved research questions.
